q: What do the first three figures of this MMSI, 237, tell a rescue centre?
a: The country where the yacht is registered
o: The type and size of the vessel
The sea area the yacht is sailing in
The year the radio was installed
why: The first three figures are the MID, the country code of the ship's flag.

q: You are looking through your DSC directory. Which of these numbers belongs to a coast station?
why: A coast station MMSI starts with 00; a group MMSI with a single 0; a ship's with its MID.

q: You buy a DSC handheld and the shop asks for the MMSI to programme it. How many figures will it have?
o: Seven
Eleven
Six
why: Every MMSI has nine figures.

q: Your DSC set has no GPS connected and no position has been entered. If you send a distress alert, what will be missing?
o: Your MMSI
The word distress
Your flag country
why: Without a GPS feed or a manual position, the alert says who you are but not where.

q: A guest on your charter yacht wants to put "his own MMSI" into the radio for the week. What do you tell him?
a: No — the MMSI belongs to the yacht and its radio licence
o: Yes — the MMSI belongs to whoever is skipper aboard
Yes, but only for the length of the charter
Yes, if he also changes the yacht's call sign
why: An MMSI is issued to the vessel with its ship radio licence, not to a person.

q: You know your friend's MMSI and want to call her yacht by DSC for a chat. What do you do?
a: Individual call to her MMSI, proposing 72; talk on 72
o: All-ships call proposing 72, then talk on 72
Individual call to her MMSI, then talk on 70
Group call to her MMSI, then talk on 16
why: A routine individual call goes to one MMSI and proposes an intership channel for the voice part.

q: Your friend's set acknowledges your DSC call, which proposed channel 72. What happens next?
a: Both sets go to 72 and you talk by voice
o: You carry on the chat as DSC text on 70
Both sets go to 16 and you talk there
You must now call her again by voice on 16
why: After the acknowledgement both sets switch to the proposed channel for the voice call.

q: Your set rings and shows this. What do you do?
a: Go to 72 (the set may switch itself) and listen for the lead
o: Ignore it — group calls are only used for tests
Reply to the lead by voice on channel 70
Call the lead on 16 to ask what it is about
why: A group call reaches every set with that group MMSI and sends them all to the proposed channel.

q: You want to ask the boats around you whether anyone has a spare impeller. Should you send an all-ships DSC call?
a: No — all-ships DSC calls are kept for emergencies and safety
o: Yes — an all-ships routine call is the right tool
Yes, as long as you select low power first
Yes, if you propose channel 16 for the replies
why: All-ships DSC calls are for distress, urgency and safety; routine calls go to one MMSI or a group.

q: Before leaving harbour you see this on the DSC set. What do you do?
a: Switch on the GPS feed, or enter the position by hand
o: Nothing — the MMSI tells rescuers where you are
Test the link by pressing the distress button
Move the DSC watch from channel 70 to 16
why: A distress alert carries your position only if the set has a GPS feed or an up-to-date manual entry.

fig.title: DSC display
lines: Plotter switched off at the breaker

q: You have decided to send a DSC distress alert. How do you work the red button?
a: Lift the cover, then press and hold it for about 5 seconds
o: Press it once briefly, like a doorbell
Hold it down while you speak the MAYDAY
Press it three times quickly in a row
why: The distress button sits under a cover and must be held for a few seconds, which prevents accidents.

q: You are about to send a DSC distress alert and have a minute to spare. How do you use it on the set?
a: Select "Flooding" as the nature of distress, then send
o: Enter the coastguard's MMSI, then send
Choose an intership channel, then send
Select "All ships, routine", then send
why: If there is time, choose the nature of distress from the menu so rescuers know what to bring.

fig.title: Holed below the waterline
lines: Water coming in faster than the pumps
About a minute before you must act

q: No acknowledgement has arrived yet. What is the set doing, and where should you be listening?
a: It repeats the alert by itself; you stay on 16
o: It has given up; you resend the alert by hand
It waits on 70; you speak your MAYDAY there
It has stopped DSC; you call for help on 72
why: A DSC set repeats a distress alert every few minutes until acknowledged, and sits on 16 for voice.

q: You are deep in a chat on 72 with dual watch switched off. Will your fixed DSC set still receive a distress alert?
a: Yes — it keeps a separate watch on channel 70
o: No — DSC only works while the set is on 16
No — only if dual watch includes channel 70
Only if the alert comes from a coast station
why: A fixed DSC set has its own receiver that listens on 70 whatever voice channel you use.

q: You want to check that your DSC works before a passage. How do you test it?
a: Send an individual call to a friend's MMSI and see it arrive
o: Send a distress alert, then cancel it at once
Make an all-ships call proposing channel 72
Call your friend by voice on channel 70
why: Test DSC with a routine individual call; never test with the distress button.

q: There is no time to choose anything from the menu: you lift the cover and hold the button. What does the alert carry?
a: An undesignated distress, with your MMSI and position
o: Nothing — it will not go without a nature chosen
Only your position, without your MMSI
A routine call to the nearest coast station
why: Sent straight from the button, the alert goes as undesignated distress with your MMSI and position.

q: What do you do now?
a: Cancel it on the set if it can, then tell all stations on 16
o: Switch the radio off and say nothing more
Wait for the coastguard to call you first
Send a second alert to cancel the first
why: Cancel a false alert by DSC where the set allows, then by voice to all stations on 16.

fig.title: False alert
lines: A child pressed the red button

q: Your DSC set sent a false distress alert at 1420 UTC. Which voice message do you send on 16?
a: "All stations ×3, this is Aurora, MMSI and position, cancel my distress alert of 1420 UTC"
o: "MAYDAY ×3, this is Aurora, MMSI and position, our MAYDAY of 1420 UTC is cancelled"
"PAN-PAN ×3, this is Aurora, MMSI and position, our alert of 1420 UTC was a mistake"
"SÉCURITÉ ×3, this is Aurora, MMSI and position, disregard our alert of 1420 UTC"
why: A false alert is cancelled to ALL STATIONS with your name, MMSI, position and the time of the alert.

q: Your set sounds an alarm and shows this. What do you do first?
a: Silence the alarm, note the details, listen on 16
o: Acknowledge the alert by DSC straight away
Relay the alert by DSC to all ships at once
Call the yacht by voice on channel 70
why: Note the alert and listen on 16; acknowledging a DSC distress alert is normally left to the coast station.

q: What does this mean, and what do you do?
a: No DSC call or alert can go out; have the base fix it before you sail
o: Alerts still go, just without a name; sail as planned
Enter any nine figures yourself so the button works
Use the flotilla's group MMSI as your own for the week
why: Without the yacht's MMSI a DSC set cannot send calls or alerts; the base must programme it.
